ELI5: How does Windows compatibility mode work?

Its called Shim Infrastructure.

To explain it you need a little 2 cent tour of how Windows programs can work, a program can make use of functions in Windows by whats called an import table (think of it like a directory listing for code). Now as Windows evolves and new standards, compatibility, a change in code strategy, dynamic changes in the way windows operates etc then where things are kept and what they look like at those indexes might be vastly different and when an old program tries to use an index that doesn't point to what it needs you get quirky behavior and or crashes.

Shims basically exploit this indexing function to intercept and redirect the import tables (lets say some XP specific code) towards alternatives which the program can then use to get its work done. Its done like this so Windows doesn't have to have lots and lots of old (potentially exploitable, buggy or inefficient) code and still maintain compatibility with programs that require it.

I'm really glossing over the details and probably making mince meat out of it but I hope you understand its not emulation its more like interpretation, program says it wants something very spesific and the shim says "he means this" and Windows replies "oh okay yeah here"

Normally the program would do something like this (program) <-> (old import table) <-> (windows) = misbehaving program

In compatibility mode it would look like this (program) <-> (old import) <-> (shim redirect) <-> (windows) = working program.

There's already an explanation here, but I'll try to make it more ELI5-friendly.

When a program wants to do something like saving a file, changing its window title, changing screen resolution, globally watching for hotkeys, etc., it asks the OS to do it by calling an appropriate function. Suppose Windows has a function saveFile(folder, name, extension, content).

OSes change over time though. For example, saveFile may be renamed, moved to some other place that you need to explicitly require, merged into some more general function, etc. For example, it may become saveFile(path, content), where path is now a full path with the file name. Your program will fail if it tries to use it the old way.

Generally such changes are made to optimize the system, so new programs should use the most recent ways to communicate with the OS, but Windows supports the old, less optimal way, in case you have some old program that doesn't work anymore. And it's called "compatibility mode" which you can manually enable for each program.

Edit: and yes, more often than not, this will help system to redirect calls to the right functions with the right arguments. Usually it doesn't mean that the old function is preserved along with the new one.

From the part number all I could determine is that the display is a seven segment vacuum fluorescent display (VFD). I could not find a pinout or complete drive specs. Since it is a VFD, it will require a special driver chip and higher than logic level voltages to operate. Having played around with VFDs before, they can usually be played with enough to figure out their pinouts. Many times you can see through the glass what pins connect to segments and grids. This article can provide you with some ideas on how to work with the display and even get around the driver chip and high voltage requirements. Being only seven segment, your display should be easier to work with as there is less going on inside it. It should only be a matter of finding the seven pins that make up the segments and then the pins for each grid above the digits and finally the filament pins. Just be sure to keep your filament power low or they will overheat and burn through. AC works best for the filaments, but it's not a hard requirement.
